{{Short description|British mathematician}}
{{Use British English|date=December 2013}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2025}}

'''Charles George Broyden''' (3 February 1933 &ndash; 20 May 2011) was a mathematician who specialized in [[optimization]] problems and [[numerical linear algebra]].<ref name="Ford2011">{{cite journal| last=Ford | first=John |title=Charles Broyden, 1933-2011|url=http://www.netlib.org/na-digest-html/11/v11n22.html#1| journal=NA Digest | volume=11 | issue=22 | date=2011-05-30}}</ref><ref name="Burdakov2011">{{cite journal| last=Burdakov | first=Oleg |author2=John Dennis |author3=Jorge More |title=Charles Broyden, 1933-2011|url=http://www.netlib.org/na-digest-html/11/v11n22.html#1| journal=NA Digest | volume=11 | issue=22 | date=2011-05-30}}</ref><ref name="Grant1970">{{cite book| last=Grant | first=John | year=1970 | title=Who's Who of British Scientists 1971/72 | isbn=978-0-582-11464-7 | page=115}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burdakov|first1=Oleg|last2=Dennis|first2=John|last3=Moré|first3=Jorge|year=2011|title=Charles G. Broyden, 1933–2011|url=http://www.mathopt.org/Optima-Issues/optima86.pdf|journal=Optima, the Newsletter of the Mathematical Optimization Society|volume=86|page=10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231203022634/https://www.mathopt.org/Optima-Issues/optima86.pdf|archive-date=2023-12-03|url-status=dead}}</ref> While a physicist working at [[English Electric Company]] from 1961 to 1965, he adapted the [[Davidon–Fletcher–Powell formula]] to solving some nonlinear systems of equations that he was working with, leading to his widely cited 1965 paper, "A class of methods for solving nonlinear simultaneous equations".<ref name="Burdakov2011"/> He was a lecturer at [[Aberystwyth University|UCW Aberystwyth]] from 1965 to 1967.<ref name="Grant1970"/> He later became a senior lecturer at [[University of Essex]] from 1967 to 1970,<ref name="Grant1970"/> where he independently discovered the [[BFGS method|Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) method]].<ref name="Ford2011"/> The BFGS method has then become a key technique in solving nonlinear optimization problems. Moreover, he was among those who derived the symmetric rank-one updating formula, and his name was also attributed to Broyden's methods and Broyden family of quasi-Newton methods.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Charles Broyden Prize |url=http://explore.tandfonline.com/page/est/charles-broyden-prize |website=Charles Broyden Prize |publisher=Taylor & Francis |access-date=31 October 2018 |archive-date=9 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190309001928/http://explore.tandfonline.com/page/est/charles-broyden-prize |url-status=dead }}</ref> After leaving the University of Essex, he continued his research career in the Netherlands and Italy, being awarded the chair at [[University of Bologna]]. In later years, he began focusing on numerical linear algebra, in particular conjugate gradient methods and their taxonomy.<ref name="Ford2011"/>

Broyden died from complications of a severe stroke at the age of 78. He was survived by his wife, Joan, and their three children Chris, Jane and Nick.<ref name="Ford2011"/>

A Charles Broyden Prize was established in 2009 to "honor this remarkable researcher" by Optimization Methods and Software in the international optimization community.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Andreas |first1=Griewank |title=Obituary for Charles Broyden |journal=Optimization Methods and Software |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=343–344 |doi=10.1080/10556788.2011.598310 |year=2011 |s2cid=27201690 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
